faq.a: Repetitive use of the wrist extensors for planting, weeding, and harvesting overloads the tendon origin.
faq.q: Why is tennis elbow common in farmers?

faq.a: Yes, septic tenosynovitis can mimic tendinopathy but is accompanied by fever, warmth, and rapid progression.
faq.q: Can an infection cause lateral elbow pain?

faq.a: No; diagnosis is clinical. Ultrasound or X‑ray is reserved for atypical cases or to rule out fracture.

exam: What bedside test distinguishes lateral epicondylitis from medial epicondylitis? — Cozen's test elicits lateral pain; medial pain is reproduced by resisted wrist flexion.
A farmer presents with lateral elbow pain after harvesting; no fever. What is your next step? — Perform Cozen's test and assess activity history; imaging only if atypical.
How does poor vascularity of the common extensor tendon affect healing? — Limited blood flow delays collagen repair, making conservative therapy longer.
Why should NSAIDs be used cautiously in a patient with active peptic ulcer disease? — NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandins, increasing ulcer risk; consider paracetamol or topical agents.
What are the red‑flag features that would change management from conservative to urgent? — Rapid swelling, fever, neurovascular deficit, or suspicion of rupture.
Explain why corticosteroid injection may be avoided in a patient with uncontrolled diabetes. — Steroids raise blood glucose and risk infection; opt for physiotherapy or NSAIDs.

How would you differentiate lateral epicondylitis from radial tunnel syndrome? — Lateral epicondylitis pain is localized to the epicondyle and worsens with wrist extension; radial tunnel pain is distal, radiates down the forearm, and is reproduced by resisted supination.
In a setting without ultrasound, how can you confirm the diagnosis? — Rely on history, palpation tenderness 1‑2 cm distal to the epicondyle, and positive Cozen’s test.
ai.title: Lateral Epicondylitis (Tennis Elbow)
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: Lateral epicondylitis is an overuse injury of the common extensor tendon origin at the lateral epicondyle. It presents with lateral forearm pain worsened by gripping. Understanding anatomy guides diagnosis and management, especially where imaging is limited.

b: Most common in adults 30‑55 years, especially manual workers and racket sport players.
Often bilateral in low‑resource settings due to repetitive agricultural tasks.
sections.p: Lateral epicondylitis is a tendinopathy of the common extensor tendon origin on the lateral humeral epicondyle, caused by repetitive wrist extension and forearm supination.

b: Extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) is the primary pain generator.
Tendon fibers become disorganized and micro‑tears develop.
sections.p: The lateral epicondyle is a bony prominence on the distal humerus. The common extensor tendon (origin of extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor digitorum, extensor carpi ulnaris) inserts here.

b: Radial nerve injury is rare but can mimic pain spread.
Lateral collateral ligament is intact; instability suggests other pathology.
sections.p: Immediately deep to the common extensor tendon lies the lateral collateral ligament complex and the radial nerve branch (deep branch of the radial nerve). The overlying skin is thin, making tenderness easy to detect.

b: Poor blood supply predisposes to chronic tendinopathy.
sections.p: The lateral epicondyle receives branches from the radial recurrent artery and the posterior branch of the profunda brachii artery, providing limited vascularity to the tendon insertion.

b: Pain referral follows the radial nerve distribution.
sections.p: Sensory innervation of the lateral elbow skin is via the lateral antebrachial cutaneous branch of the musculocutaneous nerve; deep structures receive proprioceptive fibers from the radial nerve.

b: ECRB stabilises the wrist during gripping.
Loss of tendon integrity reduces grip strength.
sections.p: The common extensor tendon enables wrist extension and forearm supination, essential for gripping, lifting, and many agricultural tasks.

b: Pain on resisted wrist extension with the elbow extended (Cozen's test).
Tenderness 1‑2 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle.
Pain on the “chair lift” maneuver (patient lifts a chair using the affected arm).
sections.p: Patients report lateral elbow pain that worsens with gripping, wrist extension, or lifting objects. In low‑resource settings, the condition may be misattributed to malaria‑related arthralgia or herbal poultice irritation.

t.b: Does pain reproduce on resisted wrist extension? Positive test confirms extensor tendon involvement.
Passive wrist flexion with elbow extended provokes pain; helps differentiate from medial pathology.

b: No fever, weight loss, or night sweats → unlikely infection or TB.
Normal radial pulse and sensation rule out vascular or nerve compromise.
sections.p: Key bedside steps: focused history of repetitive activity, inspection for swelling, palpation of the lateral epicondyle, and functional tests (Cozen, Mill). Absence of systemic signs points to a mechanical tendinopathy.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in pain with swelling suggesting a rupture or infection.
Fever, chills, or progressive weakness indicating possible septic tenosynovitis.
